q: Which statement about laparoscopy in children is FALSE?
o: Dynamic pulmonary compliance increases
Veress access fails more often than open
Pain is not lower after lap hernia repair
Visceral injury may show no peritoneal signs
e: Physiology: end-tidal CO2 rises (absorption, reduced ventilation from diaphragm pressure); dynamic compliance falls; SVR rises with sympathetic response; GFR and urine output fall; intracranial pressure rises (rarely relevant); vagal bradycardia (atropine/glycopyrrolate, self-limited); cardiac index falls above 10 mmHg; mortality with congenital heart disease is no different. CO2 blunts systemic and local inflammation (lower CRP, IL-6), lowering pain and fatigue but masking peritoneal signs of visceral injury. Length-of-stay benefit is shown for pyeloplasty, reimplantation, appendicovesicostomy and augmentation, not hernia/hydrocele (pain may be higher). Scar location matters more than size; single-site gives no cosmetic gain after 18 months. Absolute contraindications: cannot tolerate pneumoperitoneum, or surgeon cannot do it MIS; babies under a week have had it. Major access injuries are rare with either technique, but Veress fails more often. Infants: small space, pliable wall, cardiopulmonary changes; small instruments trade off versatility.
b: Compliance falls; ETCO2 rises; urine output falls
Veress: more access failure than open
No LOS benefit for lap hernia/hydrocele
Scar site > size; single-site no gain at 18 months

q: Which statement about port sites and access complications in children is FALSE?
o: Gas embolism can lower or raise end-tidal CO2
Left common iliac vein is at risk at Veress entry
3-mm port sites can be left unclosed
The aortic bifurcation may lie below the umbilicus
e: Close all port sites: omental herniation occurs even through 3 mm, with no 'safe' location; it may present with lethargy and a bulge without peritoneal signs. Umbilical fascial openings exist in children and up to 25% of adults. The umbilicus is a poor guide: the bifurcation is below it in up to 40% (more in Trendelenburg); the left common iliac vein is usually the most superior vessel there (retroperitoneal haematoma: never dilate the tract). Air/CO2 embolism: collapse with raised or lowered end-tidal CO2; place left lateral decubitus. No standardised laparoscopic/robotic curriculum exists for urologists (FLS exists in general surgery); simulation, standardised assessment, feedback and warm-up help; new instruments, robotics and AI will improve safety. (Book outline then lists chapters 28–37.)
b: Bifurcation below umbilicus in up to 40%
Left common iliac vein most at risk
No standard urology MIS curriculum; simulation and warm-up help

q: Which statement about bladder preparation for paediatric renal transplantation is FALSE?
o: Anuric bladders should be cycled first
Wetting justifies pre-transplant urodynamics
Do major reconstruction well before transplant
Augmentation reduces graft survival
e: Modern series show no change (even benefit) in graft survival with augmentation; positive cultures rise but significant infections do not. Goals: normal drainage, low-pressure continent reservoir, volitional emptying, no infection, fewest procedures. Many children have uropathy (obstruction, VUR, neuropathic bladder); commonest abnormality is a small, hypertonic, poorly compliant bladder. Urodynamics (capacity, compliance, emptying, sphincter) for neuropathic bladder, valves, ongoing voiding dysfunction or wetting, high-grade hydronephrosis, recurrent UTI; not for defunctionalised bladders without prior dysfunction, isolated reflux or enuresis. Cycle anuric bladders by CIC (assesses capacity, compliance and family ability); don't transplant into a diversion if the bladder may work. Boy with poor bladder: urodynamics, antimuscarinics and CIC before considering augmentation. Augment if capacity <75% expected with pressure >30 cmH2O despite 3-hourly CIC and maximal antimuscarinics. Ability to void affects need for a catheterisable stoma. Intraperitoneal surgery may need temporary switch from PD to haemodialysis.
b: Augmentation does not harm graft survival
Cycle anuric bladders with CIC first
Urodynamics: wetting, valves, neuropathic bladder, recurrent UTI
Augment if capacity <75% and pressure >30 cmH2O on max therapy
Reconstruct well before transplant; PD may need switch to HD

q: Which statement about the ureter and complications after paediatric renal transplant is FALSE?
o: MCDK alone does not need native nephrectomy
Routine ureteral stenting is evidence-based
Ureteral stenosis is the commonest problem (6%)
Extravesical reimplant is the preferred anastomosis
e: No data support routine stenting. Extravesical ureteroneocystostomy is preferred; make it nonrefluxing in children at risk of UTI or bladder dysfunction (refluxing acceptable in low-risk older children). Native nephrectomy: malignant hypertension, nephrotic protein loss, malignancy risk (Denys-Drash: Wilms), recurrent upper tract infection, massive reflux; not for MCDK. Complications: stenosis 6% (usually distal, at reimplant), leak 3% (early, rising drain output), stones 2% (up to 5%), significant reflux 2%. Transplant reflux with pyelonephritis is riskier than native reflux and associated with graft loss: redo reimplant or transplant-to-native ureteroureterostomy (effective). Distal stricture with some graft ureter: psoas hitch; whole ureter lost: Boari or pelvis-to-native ureter. Oliguria with fluid collection and hydronephrosis: drain percutaneously and analyse (lymphocele vs urinoma). Rising creatinine with hydronephrosis: obstruction and rejection may coexist. Late UTI reflects bladder function; bladder dysfunction can also obstruct the graft.
b: Extravesical nonrefluxing reimplant if UTI/bladder risk
No nephrectomy for MCDK; yes for Denys-Drash
Graft reflux + pyelonephritis: redo reimplant or UU

q: Ten days after renal transplant, a boy is oligo-anuric with a large perigraft collection and new hydronephrosis. Next step:
o: Percutaneous drainage and fluid analysis
Open re-exploration of the graft
Immediate graft biopsy for rejection
Observe and repeat ultrasound in a week
e: Extrinsic ureteral compression by a lymphocele (or urinoma) is likely: drain and send fluid (creatinine, culture) to decide next steps; stent or nephrostomy help drainage. Leaks show early as rising drain output.

q: Which statement about DNA, RNA and proteins is FALSE?
o: Alternative splicing creates isoforms
Proteasome blockade aids cancer
G–C pairs share three hydrogen bonds
Frameshift mutations are most damaging
e: DNA: base, 2-deoxyribose (RNA has ribose, uracil), phosphate backbone; purine pairs with pyrimidine (A–T two bonds, G–C three). Transcription in the nucleus makes mRNA; translation in cytoplasm. Response elements in promoters/enhancers bind nuclear proteins, coordinating expression; book: nuclear matrix is the site of transcription. Alternative splicing includes or excludes exons (tightly regulated isoforms). Codons of three bases encode 20 amino acids with redundancy (polymorphisms may or may not change amino acids); frameshifts are most deleterious. Degradation is active: ubiquitin tags proteins for the proteasome; inhibiting this is a cancer therapy. DNA mutations can drive initiation, progression and metastasis.

q: Which statement is FALSE?
o: Deletion commonly inactivates suppressors
Amplification can activate a proto-oncogene
Methylation occurs at any cytosine in DNA
VHL causes clear cell, not papillary, RCC
e: Methylation occurs specifically at CpG cytosines; 5-methylcytosine deaminates to thymine (C→T). Promoter CpG hypermethylation silences (tumour suppressors); loss of normal methylation activates (oncogenes); sequence is unchanged. Proto-oncogene → oncogene: activating mutation, amplification, rearrangement. Suppressors restrain growth: lost by homozygous deletion, LOH plus mutation, two mutations, or LOH plus epigenetic silencing; some escape two-hit (dominant negative, haploinsufficiency); deletion is the commonest inactivation. VHL: clear cell RCC, retinal angiomas, phaeochromocytoma, CNS haemangiomas, epididymal cystadenomas, pancreatic islet tumours; germline genes may act in sporadic tumours (VHL in ccRCC). Prostate cancer linkage genes are not proven causal. Hereditary syndromes raise GU cancer risk.
b: Methylation only at CpG; C→T deamination

q: Which statement about the cell cycle is FALSE?
o: DNA damage arrests at G1/S and G2/M
TP53 is the commonest mutated cancer gene
Phosphorylated RB1 holds E2F inactive
INK4 inhibitors block cyclin D–cdk4/6
e: Cyclin–cdk phosphorylation of RB1 (and p107, p130) releases E2F, which with DP1/DP2 activates replication genes; G1→S depends on this; RB1 mutations are common in GU cancers. Cycle: G1, S, G2, M, ordered and unidirectional; cdks need cyclins that rise and are degraded phase-specifically. Checkpoints G1/S and G2/M use CDK inhibitors in response to DNA damage, contact, cytokines, hypoxia; hypoxia, nutrients and cytokines act at G1/S; DNA damage at both. INK4 blocks cyclin D–cdk4/6. TP53 arrests (via p21), repairs, or triggers apoptosis via APAF-1/caspase 9; it is the most mutated cancer gene. Checkpoint defects cause proliferation and genetic instability.

q: Which statement about DNA repair and apoptosis is FALSE?
o: Procaspases need phosphorylation
BRCA1/2 act in homologous recombination
NER repairs ultraviolet DNA damage
Bcl-2 inhibits mitochondrial apoptosis
e: Procaspases are activated by proteolytic cleavage; initiator caspases start cascades ending in executioner caspases. Intrinsic pathway: Bcl-2 family controls mitochondrial permeability and cytochrome c release (Bcl-2 inhibits; overexpressed in some GU cancers); extrinsic: death receptors, TP53-independent (attractive targets since TP53 is mutated in over half of cancers). Apoptosis eliminates unwanted cells, suppresses tumours; cancers evade it; ceramide and clusterin are possible drug targets. Repair: NER (UV, chemicals), BER (deamination, radiation, oxidation, alkylation, replication errors; main for ROS), MMR (polymerase mispairs), DSBR (ionising radiation; HR with sister chromatid or NHEJ). BRCA1/2 with RAD51/BARD1 (recruited by PCNA) act in HR. Most damage is repaired; defects drive cancer; inherited repair syndromes raise cancer risk.
b: Intrinsic: Bcl-2, cytochrome c; extrinsic: death receptors
NER: UV; BER: ROS; MMR: mispairs; DSBR: ionising radiation

q: Which statement is FALSE?
o: GWAS most implicate the 8q24 region
Isochromosome 12p marks testis cancer
TMPRSS2–ERG fusion is in ~50% of prostate cancer
Telomere loss is mainly linked to hypomethylation
e: No strong link exists between telomere loss and hypomethylation. Telomeres cap chromosomes, shorten with division and oxidative damage; the TP53/RB1 checkpoint triggers senescence or apoptosis; losing it causes crisis and instability. Most cancers have short telomeres and express telomerase (immortality; drug target). Solid tumours show aneuploidy and complex, heterogeneous rearrangements, correlating with aggressiveness: ETS fusions (prostate), MiTF/TFE translocations (RCC), i(12p) (testis, diagnostic and prognostic); BCR-ABL is CML. Copy-number change plus second-allele change marks driver genes. SNP-array GWAS: 8q24 most implicated. RNA-seq unbiasedly sequences all RNA species. Progressing low-grade bladder cancers are luminal; de novo high-grade are basal-like.
b: Telomere loss not linked to hypomethylation
i(12p): testis; ETS fusion: prostate; MiTF/TFE: RCC
Luminal (progressing low grade) vs basal (de novo high grade) bladder

q: Which statement is FALSE?
o: Sequencing detects unculturable urinary flora
Nivolumab beat everolimus in pretreated RCC
Most testis GCTs keep wild-type TP53
PBRM1 loss predicts no anti-PD-1 benefit
e: PBRM1 loss-of-function was associated with benefit from anti-PD-1 in metastatic ccRCC. CheckMate 025: nivolumab improved survival with fewer severe adverse events vs everolimus. PD-1 limits immune activity (less autoimmunity); blocking PD-1/PD-L1 boosts T cells; first-line efficacy in cisplatin-ineligible bladder cancer (now restricted by PD-L1; EV-302 standard). Urine is not sterile: sequencing finds unculturable microbiota; urinary and gut microbiomes may affect GU cancer and treatment toxicity. Most TGCTs retain DNA damage response, wild-type TP53 and apoptosis, so DNA-damaging chemo cures. Stem cells: multilineage and immortal; cancer may be maintained by a small stem cell pool, so targeting it might eradicate cancer.

q: Which statement about varicocelectomy and testis surgery is FALSE?
o: Vasal veins are spared in varicocelectomy
Post-varicocelectomy hydrocele is lymphatic
Subinguinal approach meets fewer veins
Larger varicoceles cause more damage
e: Subinguinal: more veins, artery surrounded by small veins and often branched, so use a microscope. Ligate all veins except vasal veins; gubernacular/scrotal collaterals cause 10% of recurrences. Hydrocele after varicocelectomy is from lymphatic obstruction. Larger varicoceles impair semen more. Varicocelectomy improves semen in 60–80%; pregnancy 20–60% (RCT 44% vs 10% at 1 year; microsurgical series 43% at 1 and 69% at 2 years); natural conception avoids ART risks (multiple gestation). Azoospermic men with varicocele: about half regain ejaculated sperm. Retractile testis: dartos pouch orchiopexy. Diagnostic testis biopsy: open with microscope (avoid vessels), not percutaneous. Hydrocele repair: keep a generous border around a splayed epididymis.

q: Which statement about evaluating azoospermia is FALSE?
o: Positive antisperm antibodies mean obstruction
Vasography is done only when reconstructing
CBAVD men need a testis biopsy
Biopsy suits normal testes, vasa and FSH
e: With congenital absence of the vas, biopsy always shows spermatogenesis, so it is unnecessary; MESA suits normal spermatogenesis with unreconstructable obstruction (not maturation arrest). Positive antisperm antibodies mean obstruction (biopsy unnecessary); high FSH with small soft testes means nonobstructive azoospermia. Biopsy: azoospermia with normal testes, palpable vasa, normal FSH, negative antibodies. Vasography: absolute when azoospermia, full spermatogenesis and a palpable vas; relative in severe oligospermia, high sperm-bound antibodies, low volume/motility. Do it only at reconstruction (careless vasography causes stricture, vascular injury, haematoma, granuloma; avoid non-water-soluble contrast). Sperm in vasal fluid with full biopsy: obstruction distal; none: epididymal obstruction. Seminal vesicle aspirate with sperm = at least one patent vas and epididymis. Ejaculatory ducts: confluence of vas and SV duct, opening lateral to the verumontanum; low volume needs TRUS. TURP causes reflux, epididymitis and later obstruction. Spermatogenesis must be proven before reconstruction (prior fertility suffices).
b: Biopsy: normal testes, vasa, FSH, antibodies
SV aspirate sperm = one side patent

q: Which statement about vasectomy reversal is FALSE?
o: A sperm granuloma predicts testicular-end sperm
Toothpaste vasal fluid usually contains sperm
About 85% have sperm after vasovasostomy
Late stricture shows falling motility first
e: Thick, white, toothpaste-like fluid rarely has sperm: inspect the epididymis and do vasoepididymostomy if obstructed (vasovasostomy if in doubt; only 15% with no vasal sperm regain sperm). A granuloma vents pressure, predicting sperm at the testicular end and a better prognosis regardless of interval. Vasovasostomy: ~85% sperm, just over half pregnancy; vasoepididymostomy: 50–85% sperm, about half of those pregnancy; with older end-to-end methods 25% close by 14 months, so bank sperm. Triangulation (Berger) intussusception gives 4–6 fixation points, bloodless, but fluid cannot be checked first; anastomose only to a sperm-containing tubule. Crossover for unilateral obstruction with contralateral atrophy. Large gaps: free the cord bluntly, unravel the convoluted vas. Vas transected at two sites: the middle segment fibroses. Hydrocele suggests secondary epididymal obstruction. Late stricture: motility falls then counts (prednisone may help). Retrograde ejaculation: pseudoephedrine 120 mg 90 min before, else retrieve sperm from alkalinised urine. Vasectomy causes antisperm antibodies in 60–80% but no immune complex disease. TESE for no epididymal sperm or NOA; larger tubules yield sperm in micro-TESE; cryopreserve retrieved sperm. Outcomes depend on surgeon skill.
b: Toothpaste fluid: no sperm → consider VE
Granuloma = sperm at testicular end, better prognosis
Bank sperm (25% of older VE close by 14 months)

q: Which statement about renal surgical anatomy is FALSE?
o: The SMA can be mistaken for the left renal artery
Right renal vein ligation is well tolerated
About 25% have supernumerary renal arteries
The right renal artery runs behind the IVC
e: The right renal vein lacks collaterals, so ligation loses the kidney; the left can be ligated (lumbar, gonadal collaterals). Right renal artery is posterior to the IVC; renal arteries are end arteries; veins intercommunicate. Lumbar veins enter the left (and sometimes right) renal vein posteriorly: beware when encircling. ~25% have supernumerary arteries. SMA (or rarely hepatic artery) may be mistaken for the renal artery anteriorly: identify it posterior to the vein. Ligate artery before vein, individually; a vein that does not decompress means another artery. Posterior segmental artery is the first, most consistent branch (~one-quarter of supply). Subcostal nerve lies between internal oblique and transversus; injury causes flank paresis, bulge and pain. Posterior right lumbotomy meets pelvis, then artery, then vein (UPJ repair in children or re-operative patients). Kocher: duodenum; Pringle: porta hepatis clamp; Langenbeck: liver ligaments to expose suprahepatic IVC.
b: Right renal vein: no collaterals (left has)
SMA can mimic left renal artery
Artery before vein; posterior segmental artery first branch
Subcostal nerve between internal oblique and transversus

q: Which statement about radical nephrectomy and IVC thrombus is FALSE?
o: TEE confirms thrombus level before surgery
The renal vein ostium should be excised
DHCA beyond 40 minutes risks brain injury
Routine adrenalectomy is recommended
e: Adrenalectomy only if imaging shows involvement or an upper pole tumour abuts the adrenal. Supradiaphragmatic thrombus: chevron incision with cardiopulmonary bypass and deep hypothermic circulatory arrest (DHCA); irreversible neurological effects beyond ~40 min; heparin plus hypothermia cause oozing coagulopathy (rewarming helps); mild hypothermia without arrest is an alternative. Paradoxical embolism through a PFO can be catastrophic. TEE defines thrombus level intraoperatively. Excise the renal vein ostium (wall invasion common). Thoracoabdominal incision suits large upper pole tumours with renal vein thrombus; with a solitary lung nodule in a fit man, do nephrectomy with simultaneous metastasectomy. Lymphadenectomy has questionable survival impact (consider for enlarged nodes, cytoreduction, adverse pathology). Surgery is the mainstay for kidney cancer. Preoperative embolisation: may shrink thrombus, reduce blood loss, ease dissection, allow vein-first ligation; no proven immune benefit; postinfarction syndrome (fever, pain, nausea) in up to 75%. TNM: T1a ≤4 cm, T2b >10 cm, T3a renal vein/fat, T3c IVC above diaphragm, T4 beyond Gerota. Pancreatic fistula: NG tube, parenteral nutrition, conservative care.

q: Which statement about partial nephrectomy is FALSE?
o: Single T1 tumours need radical nephrectomy
GFR <60 raises risk of renal failure
Urine leak is managed by drain and stent
Ischaemia time is the key modifiable factor
e: Elective partial nephrectomy is supported for single T1 tumours (e.g., 4 cm anywhere) with a normal contralateral kidney; an 8-cm enhancing upper pole hilar mass suits radical nephrectomy. Duration of ischaemia is the strongest modifiable risk for renal insufficiency. Solitary kidneys are high risk; extracorporeal repair with autotransplantation adds haemorrhage, thrombosis, lymphocele and stenosis risk. Non-exophytic tumours risk urine leak: keep drains, place internal stent and Foley (less reflux). GFR <60 mL/min or significant proteinuria predicts postoperative renal failure.
b: GFR <60 or proteinuria: renal failure risk

q: Which statement about outlet therapies for neurogenic storage failure is FALSE?
o: Bulking beats surgery for durability
A pubovaginal sling allows urethral access
Durasphere uses carbon-coated zirconium beads
Bladder neck closure suits a destroyed urethra
e: Injectables restore mucosal coaptation for patients unfit for bigger surgery; efficacy and durability are inferior to surgery. Durasphere: carbon-coated zirconium beads; migration of large particles was linked to injection pressure (smaller-particle EXP less so); book answer 80 μm for particle size. Goals of storage therapy: low pressure, capacity, less DO leakage, renal preservation; augmentation after failed drugs, botulinum toxin or CIC; large bowel adds metabolic change, mucus and theoretical cancer risk. Progressive MS patients may lose CIC ability: plan alternatives (CIC non-compliance after augmentation risks perforation). A tight sling gives a pop-off and transurethral access, so closure is rarely needed; closure (transvaginal approach has not lowered fistula rates) with reconstruction for catheter-destroyed urethras. Catheterisable channel: difficult urethral catheterisation, scarring, incompetence needing closure; long-term problems include catheterisation difficulty, incontinence and stomal stenosis (Leslie 2011: 39% revisions; not perforation).
b: Sling gives pop-off and urethral access

q: Which statement about emptying aids and catheters is FALSE?
o: Credé can harm upper tracts, especially with VUR
Condom catheters cause fewer UTIs than Foleys
Indwelling catheters protect compliance
Chronic catheters raise bladder cancer risk
e: Chronic catheterisation (indwelling or CIC) can still cause poor compliance and upper tract deterioration (occult DO against dyssynergia), so survey periodically. Credé (manual compression) needs low tone, >50 cmH2O generation and low outlet resistance; it is unphysiological and dangerous with VUR or poor compliance (as is Valsalva). Trigger voiding: rhythmic suprapubic tapping (7–8 every 3 s) initiates reflex contraction in SCI/NDO; it does not reduce outlet resistance in dyssynergia. Condom catheters: less bacteriuria, UTI and death than Foley, more comfortable; risks: allergy, penile oedema, pressure sores. Suprapubic catheters have similar bacteriuria/UTI to urethral. Indwelling catheters carry 8–10% cancer risk in SCI (not with CIC): gross haematuria needs full work-up. Asymptomatic bacteriuria: treat only symptoms. Incontinence-associated dermatitis: redness, oedema, bullae in skin folds, candidiasis risk; not malignant. Absorbent product choice is trial and error, cost, convenience and marketing.
b: Chronic catheters can still harm compliance
Condom catheter: fewer UTIs and deaths

q: Which statement about active surveillance for low-risk prostate cancer is FALSE?
o: PSA density >0.15 suggests hidden higher grade
About 25% harbour occult higher grade
Grade group 1 cannot metastasise
True grade progression is 10% per year
e: True progression from Gleason 3 is 1–2.3% per year; misattribution (occult higher grade, 25–30%) is far commoner. Microfocal Gleason 3 occurs in 50–60% of middle-aged men worldwide; its mutational burden is low, with oncogenic pathways normal (aberrant in pattern 4/5). GG1 does not metastasise; deaths reflect missed higher grade. Upgrading risk: PSA density >0.15, African American race, more positive cores or core involvement; none of these (or small pattern 4) excludes AS. Exclude if life expectancy <5–7 years (biopsy refusal can still be followed with MRI). Treatment by 5 years 20–30%, by 10 years 30–40%; delay does not reduce efficacy; local progression rare; PSA is a weak metastasis predictor; grade progression is the reliable trigger. Follow-up: confirmatory biopsy within 1 year, PSA every 6 months, repeat biopsy every 3–5 years; MRI and targeted biopsy may replace systematic biopsy in very low risk (NPV depends on risk). Counsel diet and lifestyle. AS is the recommended option for low risk and an option for selected intermediate risk. Update: EAU and AUA now endorse MRI in AS (before confirmatory biopsy).
b: PSAD >0.15, Black race, more cores: upgrading risk
Confirmatory biopsy in 1 year; PSA 6-monthly; biopsy every 3–5 years
